overall_structure.value: Ferrite based duplex Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steel: a δ-ferrite + γ microstructure at hot working temperature (δ-ferrite fraction larger than 50%). Because of low C (0.1–0.4%), medium Mn (3–9%) and medium Al (3–6%) contents it develops a bimodal structure consisting of clustered austenite particles (10–40%) in a coarse-grained δ-ferrite matrix. After cold rolling + intercritical annealing + austempering the final microstructure may comprise a combination of δ, γ, α, κ, martensite (M) and bainite (B) phases or some of them depending on composition and annealing parameters.

Block b0154 describes the hot-rolled duplex microstructure: δ-ferrite stringers parallel to the rolling direction with γ grains refined through recrystallization, forming a banded microstructure parallel to the rolling direction, illustrated in Fig. 12 for ferrite based duplex Fe-3.5Mn-6Al-0.4C.

phase_evolution.value: Intercritical annealing partially reverse-transforms γ to α and partitions elements between austenite and ferrite; during austempering/isothermal treatment the γ phase partially decomposes by a eutectoid reaction into α-ferrite and needle-like κ-carbide (γ → κ + α + γR), leaving retained austenite (γR) at room temperature. In hot-rolled duplex steels α-ferrite can form along δ/γ boundaries or within γ grains along dislocations, and κ-carbides may form at the δ/γ interface as a shell around austenite at low Mn/C contents.

unmapped_findings: In the austempered Fe-3.5Mn-5.8Al-0.35C ferrite based duplex steel, the thermal and mechanical stability of the austenite decreases as its size and volume fraction are increased (block b0164).

A variant heat treatment of the same Fe-3.5Mn-5.8Al-0.35C steel (cold rolled, fast cooled at 150 °C/s to 500–600 °C, then isothermally annealed for 60 min) gives a polygonal ferritic matrix recrystallized from δ-ferrite plus lamellae formed along prior γ grain boundaries containing fine α-ferrite, κ-carbide and retained austenite (γR), and non-stoichiometric κ-carbide also precipitates in the ferritic matrix (block b0164).

For duplex Fe-Mn-Al-C steels the final microstructure may comprise a combination of δ, γ, α, κ, martensite (M) and bainite (B) phases or some of them; the phase constitution, size, volume fraction and distribution can be controlled by adjusting the annealing thermal parameters combined with the preceding cold rolling and following austempering (block b0168).

Ferrite based duplex low density steels have a mixture of (δ+γ) microstructure in the hot rolled state but develop a complex mixture of (δ+γ+M+B+κ) or some of them after cold rolling and annealing, typically showing a bimodal microstructure of clustered austenite or martensite particles in a coarse-grained δ-ferrite matrix, allowing plastic deformation of the δ-matrix combined with the TRIP and/or TWIP effect of the austenite (block b0307).

For duplex steels containing less than 6% Mn, the air-cooled hot-rolled product consists of a bimodal ferrite structure with partially recrystallized bands of coarse elongated δ-ferrite and some κ-carbides on the δ-ferrite grain boundaries, together with bands of α-ferrite with smaller grains enriched with κ-carbides (produced from the original γ) and coarse κ-carbides along δ/γ interfaces; such coarse clustered κ-carbides cannot make best use of the κ-carbides (block b0161).

In a Fe-3.3Mn-6.6Al-0.2C ferrite based duplex steel, annealing at 850 °C and water quenching gives a dual phase (δ-ferrite + Martensite) microstructure, whereas quenching to 400 °C and austempering for 10 min gives a mixture of (δ-ferrite + Bainite + Martensite + Retained Austenite) with a higher elongation (block b0227).
